content:
Friday the 13th is about to get a little spookier in Kerrobert as a team of paranormal investigators prepares to spend 36 hours inside one of west-central Saskatchewan's most talked-about historic buildings.

Canadian Paranormal Expeditions is returning to the Kerrobert Courthouse on Friday, Nov. 13, for a two-night investigation into reports of unexplained activity within the century-old building.

The group has explored the courthouse before, but this visit will give investigators an extended opportunity to search for evidence of what some believe could be paranormal activity.

"That's right Spooky Fans. We are headed back to Kerrobert," group member James Cooper announced on social media.

"No better way to spend Friday the 13th ... In a haunted museum!"

A courthouse with a haunted reputation

Built in 1920, the historic Kerrobert Courthouse has long been a landmark in the community, serving several purposes over its more than 100-year history.

Today, the building houses the Kerrobert Cultural Centre, including the Kerrobert and District Museum, Courtroom Gallery and Wheatland Regional Library, along with municipal offices.

But beyond its architectural significance and historical collections, the courthouse has developed a reputation for unusual occurrences.

Over the years, stories have circulated about unexplained footsteps, strange sightings and people reporting the sensation of being touched when no one else was nearby.

While those accounts have contributed to the building's reputation, the reported paranormal activity has not been scientifically established.

For members of Canadian Paranormal Expeditions, the stories provide an opportunity to explore the building's history while investigating claims of unexplained phenomena.

Returning for a 36-hour investigation

Canadian Paranormal Expeditions has spent years exploring reportedly haunted locations throughout Saskatchewan and parts of Alberta and Manitoba.

Founder Bradley Monks previously explained that his interest extends beyond searching for ghosts to learning about the history of the buildings his team investigates.

During an earlier interview about the Kerrobert Courthouse, Monks said access to historic buildings provides an opportunity to explore places that are not always accessible to the public.

"I like that more than anything and having access to these buildings and going to places where normally public doesn't have access to and just experience it and check it out and learn about it," Monks said.

He added that hearing people's experiences and exploring the paranormal stories connected to those locations are important parts of the investigations.

The team has already completed previous investigations at the Kerrobert Courthouse, with video footage from those visits available on its YouTube channel.

Cooper recently shared a video combining footage from two earlier investigations, describing the experiences as involving significant activity.

The upcoming visit will see the group spend two nights investigating the historic building, beginning on Friday the 13th.

Historic building continues to attract attention

The courthouse is also the focus of ongoing restoration efforts aimed at preserving one of Kerrobert's most recognizable landmarks.

The municipally designated heritage building was designed by provincial architect Maurice W. Sharon and continues to serve as a cultural and community centre.

Its museum includes historic displays and former jail cells, while the old courtroom now serves as an art gallery.

For paranormal investigators, the combination of history, architecture and decades of reported unexplained experiences makes the location an intriguing place to explore.

Canadian Paranormal Expeditions has encouraged people interested in following the investigation to visit its Facebook page and YouTube channel, where footage from previous visits can be viewed.

The group has not announced public participation details for the upcoming investigation.

Whether the latest visit produces anything unusual remains to be seen, but one thing is certain: spending Friday the 13th inside a courthouse with a century of history should make for an interesting weekend.

And for anyone who believes in things that go bump in the night, Kerrobert might just be the place to listen.
